results.title: Advancing the SmallSat Digital Twin for Active Debris Removal Simulations
results.abstract: The growing density of orbital debris threatens active spacecraft and future missions. While nets, harpoons, and robotic arms show promise for cleaning up debris, they are costly and demand precise control, motivating interest in space-based lasers that use ablation to impart small velocity changes for just-in-time collision avoidance and deorbiting. To mature this approach, we extend the SmallSat Digital Twin (SSDT) to provide a high-fidelity, spacecraft-focused simulation that integrates avionics, dynamics, core Flight System (cFS) flight software, ground control (OpenC3), and new radar/optical sensor and debris models. The enhanced SSDT supports realistic detection logic (Sun/Earth exclusion, field of view, limiting magnitude), representative tumbling debris with size/reflectivity parameters, and a laser engagement model based on an impulsive momentum transfer.

results.title: Digital Engineering for Cubesats With Semantic Web Technologies
results.abstract: Digital Engineering (DE) and the digital thread, which integrates information across the system lifecycle, offer transformative opportunities for systems engineering. This paper explores the application of DE principles to cubesat design and development, leveraging the Digital Engineering Factory (DEF) developed at the University of Arizona. The DEF integrates data from multiple engineering tools into a cohesive dataset using the Violet tool, which organizes the data as a graph database aligned with the University of Arizona Ontology Stack (UAOS). We extend prior work by applying the DEF to a cubesat design project. In particular, we develop a Python-based analysis to simulate orbital decay and calculate the time required for the cubesat to deorbit. This analysis uses inputs from multiple sources and is integrated into the workflow to demonstrate how the DEF supports automated traceability and checking of consistency, correctness, and completeness. This paper details the DEF's architecture, the cubesat application, and key findings, providing a pathway for advancing DE practices in cubesat design and development. Limitations and future research directions are discussed to guide further development of semantic web technologies in DE.

results.title: Digitally-assisted Development of a Space Robotic Arm for Small Satellites Applications
results.abstract: In-space servicing, assembly, and manufacturing (ISAM) expands space-based capabilities by extending satellite lifespans and decoupling spacecraft design from launch vehicle constraints. Robotic systems are proposed to support multiple aspects of ISAM missions, from capture and manipulation to manufacturing and repair. Consequently, the rapid development and testing of diverse robotic platforms is imperative to meet the evolving demands of the new space enterprise. This paper proposes a digital engineering framework to expedite the design, development, testing, and operation analysis of space robotic platforms. Digital engineering design tools are employed to optimize design for space environment operations; additionally, traditional manufacturing methods are streamlined with integrated wireless communication; IoT (Internet of thing) capabilities enable cloud-based modification to adjust to dynamic design requirements. Leveraging Amazon Web Services cloud-based servers, a digital twin of the robotic arm will be developed to assist the project's life cycle, from design to evaluation and test. AWS IoT communication protocols enable near real-time transmission of robotic arm sensor data to its digital twin. Siemens NX CAE (Computer Aided Engineering) facilitates photorealistic physics-based simulation, optimizing robotic arm control and motion planning. The paper details the digital engineering implementation of a two-degree-of-freedom robotic arm featuring piezoelectric rotary motors, applied in a zero gravity simulation air-bearing table study.

results.title: Digital Engineering Development in an Academic CubeSat Project
results.abstract: Digital engineering is increasingly introduced for managing and supporting the development of systems for space. However, few academic teams have the competency needed to manage projects using digital engineering and systems engineering. The subject of this paper is an academic CubeSat project in which a variety of digital engineering techniques are used. The tailoring that has been applied to fit the academic environment including students from different disciplines and levels of maturity is described. This paper shows how a customized Scrum methodology for hardware and software integrated with a workflow in a digital tool environment has given positive results for both the team and the system development. This paper also discusses how to introduce new members to the team and how to train them to work with digital engineering as a multidisciplinary team. This paper presents how the systems engineering and project management activities have been integrated into the academic CubeSat project, evaluate how well this fusion worked, and estimate its potential to be used as a guide for other digital engineering projects.

results.title: Programmatic Management for the ABEX CubeSat in a Model Based System Engineering Environment
results.abstract: View Video Presentation: https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2021-0623.vidThis paper describes how the systems engineering team has applied a Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) methodology to the Alabama Burst Energetics eXplorer (ABEX) project, formerly known as the Alabama Experiment for In-situ Shielding (AEGIS). The MBSE approach is based around the development of an Integrated Systems Model (ISM) that contains a model of the system and most of the programmatic information about the project. This paper details how the programmatic aspects of the projects were adapted to be recorded and tracked in the ISM.

results.title: Effectiveness of CubeSat-Based Architectures for Active Removal of On-Orbit Rocket Bodies
results.abstract: Recent events such as the 2009 Iridium-Cosmos collision and multiple anti-satellite weapon (ASAT) tests have propelled the increasingly urgent topic of space debris management to the forefront of current engineering inquiry. Simultaneously, the so-called ?CubeSat Revolution? has significantly reduced barriers to entry for commercial and scientific space missions. Cube- Sats have demonstrated an ever-increasing potential to offer useful capabilities for a fraction of the size, mass, and power of their larger counterparts. This paper explores the relevance and effectiveness of CubeSat architectures in active space debris removal by propulsive methods. The chosen target of interest is the Zenit-2 second-stage rocket body, representative of a particularly large and prevalent family of debris objects. The debris removal mission design problem is approached from a fundamental level. First, the CubeSat architecture design tradespace is defined and outlined, including the proposed design vector, constraints, and objective function. Next, a system model and optimization methods are presented and implemented in MATLAB. Given a set of mission requirements, the algorithm arrives at an optimal or near-optimal architecture design by iterating through combinations of commercially available CubeSat components stored in a database. Results are examined for various deorbiter CubeSat designs, and key tradeoffs between architecture options are identified and explored. Finally, considering the optimized results, a discussion of the most effective propulsive solutions for Zenit-2 rocket body removal using CubeSat clusters is presented.
